why: Sizes can only go up, and moving item i up by one costs cost[i]. Sweep values upward: at each value, among all items waiting there, the most expensive one should stay and the rest move up one step and pay. A max-heap of waiting costs picks who stays, which is the exchange argument 'move the cheap ones'.
hints: Several items share a size; exactly one can keep it. Which one should, if every step up costs that item's own cost per unit?
Process values in increasing order. Every item currently at value v (original or pushed up) waits in a pool; the most expensive one settles at v, all others pay their cost to move to v+1.

Sort by size; keep a max-heap of costs and the running sum of costs in it. At each value add newcomers, pop the max, add the remaining sum to the answer, step v; jump v forward when the heap is empty. O(n log n).
pitfalls: The cost is per increment, so an item pushed up 3 steps pays 3 * cost[i] (example 2 pays 2 * 3).
Do not step v one by one across empty stretches when the heap is empty; jump to the next size or you will time out on large sizes.
statement:
You are given two arrays size and cost of length n. You may increase any size[i] by 1 as many times as you like; each single increase of item i costs cost[i]. Sizes can never be decreased.

Return the minimum total cost to make all values in size distinct.

Worked example: size = [2, 3, 3, 2], cost = [2, 4, 5, 1].

  • Two items have size 2 (costs 2 and 1) and two have size 3 (costs 4 and 5).
  • Raise item 1 (size 3, cost 4) once to 4: cost 4.
  • Raise item 3 (size 2, cost 1) three times to 5: cost 3.
  • Sizes become [2, 4, 3, 5], all distinct, total 7.
constraints:
• Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5
  • 1 ≤ size[i], cost[i] ≤ 10^9
